A giraffe’s heart weighs about 11 kg and pumps against blood pressure roughly double ours.
Giraffes have only seven neck vertebrae, the same as humans, each up to 28 cm long.
Tight skin on their lower legs works like compression stockings, stopping blood from pooling.
Valves and elastic vessels in the neck stop them blacking out when lowering their head.
A giraffe’s tongue reaches about 45 cm and is dark to resist sunburn.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve detours down the chest and back up, a route of about 4.5 m.
Hooves span up to 30 cm, and one kick can kill a lion.
Giraffes have no upper front teeth; a tough dental pad and a prehensile tongue strip leaves.
Giraffes sleep as little as 30 minutes a day, often in bursts of a few minutes.
Calves drop about 1.8 m to the ground at birth.
Newborn calves can stand within an hour and run within a day.
Roughly half of all calves die in their first year, mostly to lions and hyenas.
Mothers park calves in “crèches” guarded by a few adults while the rest go feed.
Giraffes hum at night; scientists only confirmed the sound in 2015.
Males fight by “necking,” swinging their skulls like hammers into rivals’ bodies.
Bulls’ skulls thicken with age as calcium deposits build up, turning them into heavier weapons.
Giraffes can go days without drinking, getting most of their water from leaves.
Drinking is their most vulnerable moment: legs splayed wide, they can barely flee.
Giraffes can’t trot; they switch straight from walking to galloping.
When walking, they move both legs on one side together, called pacing, unlike most hoofed animals.
Every giraffe’s coat pattern is unique, and calves inherit patterns similar to their mother’s.
Dark spots act as thermal windows: blood vessels beneath them release excess body heat.
Giraffe skin is up to 2 cm thick, thorn-proof armor for browsing acacia.
Males reach about 5.5 m tall, taller than a double-decker bus.
A giraffe’s neck alone can weigh about 270 kg.
Giraffes were long treated as one species; genetic studies now suggest four.
The okapi is the giraffe’s only living relative, a forest dweller with zebra-striped legs.
Ancient Romans called giraffes “camelopards,” believing them a hybrid of camel and leopard.
Julius Caesar displayed a giraffe in Rome in 46 BC, the first most Romans had ever seen.
Giraffe numbers fell roughly 30% in three decades, a “silent extinction.”
Giraffes’ long, sticky saliva coats the thorns they swallow with acacia leaves.
A giraffe’s tongue is prehensile and can wrap around branches like a hand.
Giraffes chew cud like cows, regurgitating food to chew it a second time.
An adult giraffe eats about 30 to 35 kg of foliage a day.
Giraffes are picky browsers, favoring acacia leaves even though the thorns are vicious.
Ossicones, the horn-like knobs, start as cartilage and fuse to the skull as giraffes mature.
Giraffes are born with ossicones lying flat, which protects the mother during birth.
Males often have bare, scarred ossicone tops from fighting; females’ stay tufted with hair.
Some bull giraffes grow an extra bony bump in the middle of the forehead with age.
A giraffe’s eyes are among the largest of any land mammal, giving excellent long-range vision.
Giraffes can spot predators from over a kilometer away thanks to their height and eyesight.
Long eyelashes shield their eyes from dust, insects, and thorns.
Giraffes can close their nostrils to keep out sand and dust.
Zebras and giraffes often graze together, since giraffes spot predators from above.
Oxpecker birds ride giraffes, eating ticks, though they also pick at open wounds.
A giraffe’s tail can reach about a meter and ends in a long black tuft for swatting flies.
Giraffes can sprint about 55 km/h over short distances.
A giraffe’s stride can cover roughly 4.5 m.
Giraffes cannot jump; a fence half a meter high can be a serious obstacle.
Giraffes’ long legs make swimming very difficult, and their necks would hamper balance in deep water.
A giraffe’s gestation lasts about 15 months, and mothers give birth standing up.
Giraffe milk is rich in fat, helping calves grow about 2.5 cm per day early on.
A calf can reach roughly 2 m tall at birth, taller than most adult humans.
Mothers fiercely defend calves, and a kick to a lion’s skull can be fatal.
Wild giraffes live about 25 years; those in zoos can reach their late 30s.
Male giraffes keep growing slowly through much of their lives.
At rest, a calf’s heart beats about 150 times a minute; an adult’s beats far slower.
Their lungs hold about 55 liters of air, far more than a human’s.
A giraffe’s windpipe is very long, so it breathes slowly to avoid rebreathing stale air.
A giraffe’s brain sits about 2 m above its heart, requiring extreme blood pressure to feed it.
Blood vessels in the neck form a rete mirabile, a network that regulates blood flow to the brain.
Giraffes have the highest blood pressure of any land animal, roughly 280/180 mmHg.
When a giraffe lowers its head, the jugular’s elastic walls and valves manage a huge shift in blood volume.
A giraffe’s stomach has four compartments, extracting maximum nutrition from tough leaves.
Giraffes need less water than most grazers because leaves provide much of their moisture.
Giraffes lick bones and soil to get calcium and phosphorus, a habit called osteophagia.
A giraffe can clean its own ears with its tongue.
Giraffes can lick their own nostrils clean with their tongue.
Giraffe tongues are dark purple, blue, or black on top and pinkish underneath.
A giraffe’s upper lip is mobile and tough, letting it pluck leaves between thorns.
Giraffe teeth wear down over time, and worn molars can shorten an old giraffe’s life.
A giraffe’s distinct smell comes from skin compounds that may repel parasites.
The reticulated giraffe has sharp polygon spots separated by bright white lines.
The Masai giraffe has darker, jagged, vine-leaf-shaped spots.
Northern giraffes’ ranges are shrinking; some populations number only in the hundreds.
The Rothschild’s giraffe, a northern subspecies, is one of the most endangered.
Giraffes once ranged across much of Africa, but habitat loss has cut their range dramatically.
Giraffe numbers have risen in some southern African countries thanks to conservation.
Poaching for meat, hides, and tail hair still threatens giraffes in parts of Africa.
Giraffe tail hair has been prized for jewelry and fly whisks, driving poaching in some regions.
Fossil relatives of giraffes like Sivatherium were bulky, moose-like animals with massive horns.
Giraffes’ ancestors had short necks; long necks evolved gradually over millions of years.
The neck may have evolved partly for fighting, not just for reaching high leaves.
The Romans, Chinese, and Egyptians all treated giraffes as exotic status gifts.
In 1414, a Bengal ruler sent a giraffe to China, where it was hailed as a mythical qilin.
In 1827, a giraffe named Zarafa was walked from Marseille to Paris, sparking “giraffomania.”
The name “giraffe” likely comes from Arabic “zarafah,” possibly meaning “fast walker” or “charming one.”
Ancient Egyptians depicted giraffes in art thousands of years ago.
Rock art across Africa shows giraffes, some dating back thousands of years.
Giraffes are highly social, living in loose, changing groups rather than fixed herds.
Female giraffes form long-term friendships and tend to associate with the same relatives.
Giraffes have been observed mourning, with mothers standing over dead calves.
Giraffes are mostly silent, but can snort, grunt, moan, and hiss.
Calves bleat, and mothers call with a moo-like sound to reunite when separated.
Giraffes spend about half the day feeding, mostly in early morning and late afternoon.
Giraffes rest standing up and only sleep lying down for short spells.
Lions are the main predators of giraffes, usually targeting calves or sick adults.
A giraffe can turn a lion attack around with a kick powerful enough to crush its skull.
Giraffes are the tallest land animals, with legs alone about 1.8 m long.
A giraffe’s neck is so long that its head can reach a second-story window.
